docs: refresh the benchmark tables and the ratios quoted around them (#574)

The committed sweep dated 2026-07-30 and predated the wasm, autolink, and
renderer work that landed since. Regenerated from the Benchmark docs
workflow on the current main so the numbers include it.

The generator only owns the block between the marker comments, so the
prose ratios derived from those tables were recomputed by hand:

  napi vs the two TS renderers, 48.7 KB   4.9-5.7x -> 4.0-5.1x parse
                                          6.7-10.6x -> 7.1-12.1x parse+render
  napi vs the two TS renderers, ~1 MB     7.3-8.3x -> 7.7-8.7x parse
                                          10.7-11.4x -> 11.4-12.0x parse+render
  native throughput at ~1 MB              223-320 -> 267-370 MB/s
  @mizchi/markdown at ~1 MB               ~1 -> ~2 ops/sec parse
                                          ~12 -> ~23 ops/sec parse+render

The native lead sentence needed rewording rather than renumbering: on
parse+render the second row is now @ox-content/napi rather than a
third-party engine, so "leads the next-fastest comparison" would have
been describing the N-API boundary against ourselves. It now names
pulldown-cmark explicitly and says what separates the top two rows.

The conformance column moves too (md4x 92.5% -> 99.5%, @tanstack 45.9% ->
47.4%). That is not new measurement: the tracked
benchmarks/commonmark-conformance/results.json already held those
figures, and it was the tables that lagged behind it.

commit.message:
feat(parser): make cjkEmphasis pair runs against CJK punctuation (#545) (#548)

* feat(parser): make cjkEmphasis pair runs against CJK punctuation

`cjkEmphasis` was a documented option that did nothing: it was plumbed from
the N-API bindings into `ox_content_transform` and stopped there, because
`ox_content_parser` never read it. Its doc comment claimed "the parser is
already CJK-friendly", which measurement contradicts — `A**強調。**B` stayed
literal, exactly as in markdown-it (commonmark), micromark, and
pulldown-cmark.

The gap is in CommonMark's flanking rules. Whether a `*`/`_` run may open or
close depends on the characters beside it, and punctuation on the outer side
blocks it. The rule reads Unicode punctuation as a whole, so East Asian
punctuation blocks it too. Latin prose rarely notices because a space usually
sits between the punctuation and the delimiter; CJK sets punctuation directly
against the preceding word, so it comes up constantly.

This gives the option an implementation: with it on, East Asian punctuation is
classified as an ordinary character when computing flanking, and nowhere else.
Scope is deliberately narrow:

- Only the fullwidth and CJK-specific blocks are reclassified. Halfwidth ASCII
  punctuation is written the same way in every script, so a Latin document
  parses identically either way — asserted by a test.
- Only the punctuation rule is relaxed. Whitespace still blocks a run, and
  U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE is whitespace, so it is unaffected.
- Off by default. It is a deviation from the specification, and the default
  profile still renders all 652 CommonMark 0.31.2 examples per spec — the
  conformance suite and the published benchmark column both still read 652/652.

Refs #545

* docs(cjk-emphasis): list every reclassified punctuation range

Co-authored-by: Codesmith <codesmith-bot@users.noreply.github.com>

Co-authored-by: Codesmith <codesmith-bot@users.noreply.github.com>

commit.message:
docs: measure and publish CommonMark conformance per engine (#545) (#547)

* docs: measure and publish CommonMark conformance per engine

The speed tables rank strict and deliberately-non-strict parsers together,
which is only a fair comparison if the reader can see which is which. Adds a
measured `CommonMark` column to every row, sourced from a new sweep in
`benchmarks/commonmark-conformance/`.

The rate is measured rather than asserted. Two decisions make it fair, and
both are load-bearing:

- Each engine runs in the most spec-faithful mode it exposes, not in its
  benchmark defaults. `markdown-it`/`markdown-it-ts` use their `commonmark`
  presets, `micromark` and `remark-html` are told to pass raw HTML through,
  and `md4w` runs with `parseFlags: 0`. Measured with benchmark defaults
  those four score 88–92%, which would report the preset rather than the
  engine. Engines exposing no such mode are scored as they ship.
- Both sides pass through `normalize_html`, the normalizer the in-repo
  conformance suite already uses, reached through a new `--normalize` filter
  on the native competitor binary so JS and native engines are judged
  identically. Byte-exact comparison ranks engines by markup spelling:
  ox-content scores 82.5% exact and 100% normalized purely because it adds
  slug `id` attributes to headings. `pulldown-cmark` scoring 100% under the
  normalizer is the check that it is not tuned to one engine.

The published speed numbers are untouched — the tables were re-rendered from
the figures already committed, not re-measured on a different host.

Also corrects two overstatements the sweep turned up while checking the CJK
claims in the issue:

- `cjkEmphasis` is documented as if it enables something. It does not change
  parsing, and the parser is not CJK-friendly beyond what CommonMark already
  allows: `A**強調。**B` stays literal in ox-content exactly as it does in
  `markdown-it` (commonmark), `micromark`, and `pulldown-cmark`.
- `syntax-extensions.md` claimed emphasis adjacent to CJK is "a case where
  many CommonMark parsers need manual workarounds", and illustrated it with
  an example that is not punctuation-adjacent.

Contrary to the issue, ox-content does target strict CommonMark: 652/652 core
profile, with the three GFM-profile differences being the autolink extension.
That is now stated in the README and docs rather than left implicit.

Refs #545

* fix: pin patched brace-expansion to clear GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895

* fix: validate competitor CLI args and qualify conformance wording

commit.message:
docs: refresh benchmark numbers (#526)

Applied from the Benchmark docs workflow artifact (run 29650892324:
blacksmith-32vcpu-ubuntu-2404, Bun 1.3.14, median of 3 runs, dispatched
on a quiet benchmark queue after the native competitor rows landed).

First refresh since the workflow revival, so the tables pick up
everything at once: today's parser/renderer/mdast optimizations, the
Bun.markdown row, and the new native rows (pulldown-cmark, Grok Build's
markdown stack, and boundary-free ox-content). Headlines at 48.7 KB:
parse 400.5 MB/s native / 199.8 MB/s through napi; parse+render 270.3
native, with the napi row (228.4) ahead of pulldown+push_html (225.0)
and Bun.markdown (187.8).

An earlier artifact from run 29646906075 was discarded: it predated the
native rows and its absolute numbers were depressed ~3x by concurrent
PR benchmark runs on the same account.
